nameStory: This orchid is named after botanist Howard Shriver, who likely contributed to our understanding of these delicate plants. The 'frilly' part of its name comes from the beautifully fringed petals that give the flowers a delicate, ruffled appearance like tiny purple tutus.
description: Shriver's frilly orchid is an extremely rare native orchid that produces a spike of purple flowers with distinctively fringed petals. This slender plant typically grows 1-3 feet tall with a single flowering stalk rising from basal leaves. It's one of North America's rarest orchids, making any sighting a truly special discovery. The plant belongs to the bog orchid group, known for their intricate flower structures and specific habitat needs.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Purple flowers arranged in a dense cylindrical spike, each bloom featuring deeply fringed petals that feel delicate and papery to the touch, creating a frilly, ruffled appearance

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Lance-shaped leaves that clasp the stem, decreasing in size as they move up the plant, with a smooth, waxy feel and parallel veins typical of orchids

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Single upright stem growing 1-3 feet tall, emerging from a cluster of basal leaves, with the distinctive orchid symmetry in its flowers

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Smooth, sturdy green stem that feels firm and slightly succulent, supporting the weight of the flower spike without bending

habitat: This critically rare orchid is found in specialized wetland habitats including bogs, wet meadows, and marshy areas with consistent moisture. It prefers acidic, nutrient-poor soils and may be associated with sphagnum moss and other bog plants. Given its extreme rarity, specific habitat details in New England are closely guarded by conservation groups.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge from the ground in late spring, forming the basal rosette that will support the eventual flower spike.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming occurs in mid to late summer, when the spectacular fringed purple flowers open and release their subtle, sweet fragrance to attract pollinators.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and seed capsules develop, while leaves begin to yellow and prepare for dormancy as the plant stores energy in underground tubers.
seasonality.winter: Plant dies back completely underground, surviving as dormant tubers buried in the bog soil until spring warmth triggers new growth.

funFact: This orchid is so incredibly rare that it's considered critically imperiled, meaning you're more likely to spot a celebrity than find one of these plants in the wild - making any encounter a once-in-a-lifetime botanical treasure hunt!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with other purple fringed orchids in the same genus, particularly the Greater and Lesser Purple Fringed Orchids. Look for the specific fringe pattern on the petals and the overall flower spike shape - Shriver's has its own unique frilly signature that botanists can distinguish with close examination.
contextualKnowledge: Due to its critically imperiled status, exact locations of Shriver's frilly orchid populations are typically kept confidential by botanists and conservation organizations. If you think you've found one, contact local botanical experts rather than sharing the location publicly, as these plants need protection from collection and habitat disturbance.
compareHints: Among its Platanthera relatives, Shriver's frilly orchid is distinguished by its particular fringe pattern and purple coloration. While it shares the fringed petal characteristic with Greater and Lesser Purple Fringed Orchids, the specific arrangement and density of the fringe, along with subtle differences in flower spike structure, help botanists tell them apart. The extreme rarity also means any purple fringed orchid in New England is more likely to be one of its more common cousins.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its bog orchid relatives, this is by far the smallest and most inconspicuous - while cousins like the fringed orchids have showy white or purple flowers, the small green wood orchid is all about stealth.

Among its Platanthera relatives, the White-fringed Orchid is distinguished by its pure white color and deeply fringed petals - the Lesser and Greater Purple Fringed Orchids have similar fringed flowers but are purple, while other white bog orchids lack the dramatic fringe.
Among New England's bog orchids (Platanthera), the Lesser Purple Fringed Orchid is distinguished by its bright purple color and deeply fringed flower lips.
White bog orchid stands out from its Platanthera relatives by its pure white color and incredibly strong clove-like fragrance.
Among its Platanthera relatives, the ragged fringed orchid stands out for its greenish-white color and extremely irregular, deeply cut fringes.
Among its Platanthera relatives, the Greater Purple Fringed Orchid stands out for its size and deeply fringed purple petals.
Among New England's bog orchids, this species is distinguished by its greenish-white flowers and self-fertilizing habit.
Among its bog orchid relatives, green bog orchid is distinguished by its consistently greenish flowers and preference for the wettest habitats.
Among its bog orchid relatives, the Round-leaved Bog Orchid is unique for having just two large, circular basal leaves.
Among New England's bog orchids, pale green orchid stands out for its particularly subtle coloring and preference for disturbed shoreline habitats.

Among New England's bog orchids, Hooker's is distinctive for having exactly two large basal leaves lying flat on the ground, while most other Platanthera species have multiple leaves arranged up the stem.
Among its bog orchid relatives, Large-leaved Bog Orchid is unmistakable due to its two massive basal leaves - most other Platanthera species have smaller, more numerous leaves arranged up the stem.
Among its bog orchid relatives, the orange-fringed orchid is the only one with orange flowers and deeply fringed petals.
Among New England's bog orchids, this is the only one with such intensely bright orange flowers in a dense, compact cluster.

Unlike its relatives the round-leaved bog orchid (which has two large round leaves) or Hooker's orchid (which has two broad leaves that hug the ground), the blunt-leaved rein orchid typically has just one distinctively paddle-shaped leaf with a rounded tip.
